text.en: Shalini lives in a town in Kerala. Her aunt Acchamma lives nearby with a daughter, Chinni, whom Shalini calls her sister. When Acchamma learned that Shalini's uncle was facing money trouble before a festival, the family shared what they had. This is how families support each other. In this chapter we study families and communities.

A joint family has several generations living together: grandparents, parents, uncles, aunts, brothers, sisters and cousins. A nuclear family has only parents and children. In many Indian languages there is no word for cousin, because cousins are called brothers and sisters, which shows the deep bonds among all the children in a family. Some people choose nuclear families because of jobs, studies or the pace of modern living, but family ties remain.
Family relationships are based on love, care, cooperation and interdependence. Grandparents tell stories with humour and wisdom, parents provide and guide, and children help at home as they grow. Following our dharma, or doing our duty, has long been an important principle of Indian culture. Each member has responsibilities, and each receives support. Families decide things together, share special expenses and look after the old and the young. This is a school of values.
A group of connected people who live in the same area or share work or interests may be called a community. We belong to many communities: neighbourhood, school, clubs and groups of friends. Over time communities agreed upon practices on sharing water, grazing land and forest produce. These rules were rarely written but gave everyone secure access to resources. Communities also help in need. Around Jhabua in Madhya Pradesh, villagers facing a water crisis built structures to save rain water, working as a duty to the community and the environment, without pay.
Kamal Parmar, who ran a small workshop in Ahmedabad, noticed children on the street who did not go to school. He started classes for them, 150 children joined regularly and older students volunteered as teachers. In cities the community is more complex because everyone depends on many people and groups. Residents can agree on rules for cleanliness, waste and the care of common areas. Respect, cooperation and responsibility keep communities strong and make life better for all.

problem.en: Make a list of ways your family and your community help each other.

text.en: Family: sharing chores and caring for elders.
Community: keeping streets clean and sharing water.
Both rely on cooperation and duty.

prompt.en: How do family and community build values in a child?

requiredIdeas.en: Love, care and cooperation at home.
Duty to others in the neighbourhood.
Shared rules and helping each other.

commonMisconceptions.en: Thinking that only nuclear families are modern.

points.en: A joint family has several generations; a nuclear family has parents and children.
Dharma, or duty, guides family life.
Communities share resources by agreed rules and help each other.
Volunteers like Kamal Parmar show community service.
